newsitem.title: UK: BA's Ayling battles on all fronts.
newsitem.headline: BA's Ayling battles on all fronts.

text.p: For a man whom even the left-leaning Guardian newspaper calls a "nice, liberal-minded businessman", British Airways Plc's chief executive Robert Ayling is stirring up demons.

In recent days Ayling has been alternately slammed and lauded in the British press as a common bully, a technocrat, a man with terrier-like tenacity and a leader who likes to keep his management team "in a state of creative apprehension".

In just 18 months at the top of the self-styled World's Favourite Airline, the energetic 50-year-old has set in train initiatives as momentous and aroused controversy as great as anything in its 78-year history.

These include proposing an ambitious alliance with American Airlines which has caused terror and rage among BA's long-haul competitors and set off a tricky round of negotiations with European competition authorities.
He will also be remembered as the man who dropped the British flag from the tail of his planes and replaced it with a heady ethnic mix including Polish folk art and African beadwork.

But it is his billion pound cost-cutting package, announced last September, which is at the root of current bloodletting at the airline, which Ayling is determined should remain one of the most successful and profitable in the world.
Moves to restructure pay for cabin crews and sell off BA's catering operations have mired the company in a public relations nightmare, and threaten to cost it tens of millions of pounds.

But those close to Ayling say he is resolute about securing the long-term survival of BA in a market which is becoming increasingly competitive, with a plethora of low-cost operators squeezing ticket prices at the bottom and the gradual emergence of dominant super-alliances between major players at the top.

According to its own figures, BA is the world's largest international passenger airline. It has also been one of the most consistently profitable since its privatisation in 1987, posting pre-tax profits of 640 million pounds ($1.1 billion) in the 12 months to March.

The airline, which traces it origins back to the first hair-raising scheduled flights between London and Paris in 1919, is far removed from the dowdy state-owned business which former Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher's favourite businessman Lord King was brought in to turn around in 1981, when it was losing around half a billion pounds a year.
Success had been built on pioneering marketing ploys such as its World Offers programme and a growing franchise business, where smaller airlines adopt BA's colours and uniforms.

It has also adopted an aggressive approach to acquisitions and alliances, buying up domestic rivals like British Caledonian and Dan Air, and taking sizeable stakes in companies including Australia's Qantas Airways Ltd, TAT European Airlines of France and USAir, although that relationship ended in May.

Despite his multiple battles, Ayling found time to pen an article in Thursday's Times newspaper in which he apologised for appearing "heavy-handed or clumsy" in handling the pay dispute with cabin staff, but said the changes he was pushing through were vital to keep BA at the top of the pile.
"We want to reach agreement with our employees and their unions and are ready to do so, but we cannot do it at the expense of BA's future competitiveness," he wrote. ($ = 0.593 British Pounds)
